mainTopic: A craftsman who strays from the owner's order (the carpenter case), and whether dye counts as something separate from the wool
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier definition: 'ugly dye' means leftover dye scraped from the pot. Then a ברייתא discusses a carpenter who made a bench when he was asked for a chair, or the reverse. רבי מאיר says the carpenter keeps the piece and pays for the wood. רבי יהודה says the owner keeps it and pays the carpenter the lower of his costs or the value he added. רבי מאיר agrees with that payment rule when the carpenter made the right item but made it badly. Next the גמרא asks whether dye on wool still counts as a real, separate thing. It tries several cases to find where this question would matter, and rejects some of them. It keeps a case where a thief returns dyed wool after the dye's price fell, and also רבינא's case of a monkey that dyed one person's wool with another person's dyes. Finally the גמרא tries to settle the question with proofs from garments dyed with ערלה and שביעית peels. Both proofs are rejected, because each of those laws has its own special rule from a verse.

steps.title: Ugly dye means leftover dye from the pot
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes defining the 'ugly dye' from the earlier case: it is the leftover dye scraped from the cauldrons.
steps.simpleTranslation: The leftover dye scraped from the bottom of the cauldrons.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the tail end of the previous discussion. The גמרא is explaining what 'ugly dye' means in the case of a dyer who did a bad job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dyer did not use fresh dye. He used what was left over in the pot from earlier jobs, so the color came out poor. That is the bad workmanship the earlier case was talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: Sediment, the leftover residue at the bottom
Cauldrons or pots (here, the dyer's vats)

phrases.english: The sediment of the cauldrons.
phrases.notes: This finishes the explanation of 'ugly dye' from the case just before: the dyer used leftover dye from the pot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a definition that began before this section starts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What counts as 'ugly' dyeing in the earlier case?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Dyeing with leftover dye sediment from the pots.

steps.title: Carpenter makes a bench instead of a chair
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a carpenter is given wood for a chair and makes a bench, or the reverse. רבי מאיר says he pays for the wood. רבי יהודה says he is paid the lower of his costs or the added value.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If someone gives wood to a carpenter to make a chair, and he makes a bench, or to make a bench and he makes a chair, רבי מאיר says the carpenter pays the owner the value of his wood. רבי יהודה says: if the added value is more than the costs, the owner pays him his costs. If the costs are more than the added value, the owner pays him the added value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a craftsman who made a different item than he was told to. רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה disagree about who keeps the item and how payment works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds that making a different item is a big enough change that the carpenter takes the item as his own and just pays for the raw wood. רבי יהודה holds that the item still belongs to the owner. Because the carpenter ignored the order, he only gets the smaller of two amounts: his expenses or the value he added to the wood.

keyTerms.meaning: The increase in value from the work

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up שֶׁבַח and יְצִיאָה. שֶׁבַח is how much more the item is worth now. יְצִיאָה is what the work cost the carpenter. Under רבי יהודה the carpenter always gets whichever amount is smaller.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic dispute about whether a craftsman who changes the job takes ownership. The very next line builds on it.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who gives wood to a carpenter
to make a chair from it,
and he made a bench from it;
or a bench, and he made a chair from it –

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: נוֹתֵן לוֹ דְּמֵי עֵצָיו.
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: He gives him the value of his wood.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
If the added value is greater than the expenses –
he gives him the expenses,
phrases.notes: Here 'he' is the owner, who keeps the item and pays the carpenter.

phrases.english: and if the expenses are greater than the added value –
he gives him the added value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related ברייתא about a craftsman who strays from his instructions, like the dyer case before it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: the carpenter pays for the wood and keeps the item. רבי יהודה: the owner keeps it and pays the lower of expenses or added value.

steps.title: רבי מאיר agrees when the right item is made badly
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if the carpenter made the right kind of item but made it ugly, רבי מאיר agrees that the owner pays the lower of expenses or added value.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מאיר agrees that if he gave wood to a carpenter to make a beautiful chair and he made an ugly chair, or a beautiful bench and he made an ugly bench, then if the added value is more than the costs, the owner pays him the costs. If the costs are more than the added value, the owner pays him the added value.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now limits רבי מאיר's view. It shows a case where he agrees with רבי יהודה's payment rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the carpenter made the correct item, a chair or a bench, just not a nice one. That is only a small change, so even רבי מאיר says the carpenter does not take the item. He gets the lower of his costs or the added value.

keyTerms.meaning: And he agrees; marks a case where an opinion agrees with the other side

steps.whatToRemember: Making a different item (bench instead of chair) is a big change, and רבי מאיר says the carpenter keeps it. Making the right item badly is a small change, and everyone agrees the owner keeps it and pays the lower of expenses or added value.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir agrees
if he gave wood to a carpenter
to make a beautiful chair from it,
and he made an ugly chair from it;
a beautiful bench, and he made an ugly bench –
if the added value is greater than the expenses,
he gives him the value of the expenses;
and if the expenses are greater than the added value,
he gives him the value of the added value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and narrows רבי מאיר's view to cases of a real change of item.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the right item is made poorly, even רבי מאיר agrees the owner keeps it and pays the lower of expenses or added value.

steps.title: Is dye a separate thing from the wool?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the improvement that dye gives wool counts as its own separate thing, or whether we only see dyed wool.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: Is the improvement from dye on wool treated as something real and separate, or is the improvement from dye on wool not treated as separate?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about the dyer cases. It asks how to view the dye once it is on the wool.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One option: the dye stays its own separate thing sitting on the wool. The other option: the dye blends in, and all we have is colored wool. The question is asked here and not yet answered, so the next lines will try to settle it.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked of them; introduces an open question

phrases.english: A question was asked of them:
Is there improvement of dyes on the wool,
phrases.notes: In other words: does the dye stay a separate thing on the wool?

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵין שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל הַצֶּמֶר?
phrases.english: or is there no improvement of dyes on the wool?
phrases.notes: Meaning the dye does not stay separate, and we just look at it as colored wool.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: יֵשׁ שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל הַצֶּמֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the dye and wool topic and opens a new question about how to view dye.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the dye count as a separate thing on the wool, or is it just part of the colored wool?

steps.title: What case is the question about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the dye question is about. It first suggests a thief who stole raw dye materials, ground them, soaked them, and dyed wool with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? Suppose someone stole dye materials, ground them up, soaked them, and dyed wool with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It asks where the dye question would really matter and offers a first possible case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A question only matters if there is a real case where the answer changes the outcome. The first case offered is a thief who stole raw materials and processed them himself before dyeing.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?
If you say (a suggestion the גמרא is about to test)
Dyes, or the raw materials used to make dye
And he soaked them (in water to make dye)

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say that he stole dye materials
and ground them and soaked them
and dyed with them,
phrases.notes: Both bracketed words mean 'with them.' The square-bracket word is the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for a real case where the question from Step 4 would matter.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The case in which the question of whether dye counts as a separate thing on wool makes a practical difference.

steps.title: In that case the thief already owns the dye through change
steps.stepSummary: The first case does not work. Grinding and soaking changed the materials, so the thief already acquired them through שינוי. He simply owes their value, whatever we say about dye on wool.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then you can settle it another way: he acquired them through the change he made.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the first suggested case. The dye question does not matter there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thief who changes a stolen item acquires it and pays its value from the time he stole it. The thief already changed the materials when he ground and soaked them. So the dye question plays no role in that case.

keyTerms.meaning: Derive it instead from (another, simpler reason)
A change in the stolen item, which makes it the thief's property (he then pays its value)

phrases.english: Derive it instead
from the fact that he acquired them through change!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the case suggested in Step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the suggested case, not the question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In that case שינוי already decides the outcome, so the dye question changes nothing.

steps.title: The case: dye that was already soaked
steps.stepSummary: The question is about a thief who stole dye that was already soaked and ready, then dyed with it. He made no change of his own. Is the dye still a separate thing the owner can demand, or is it lost inside the wool so the thief can say he has nothing of the owner's?
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the case is where he stole dye that was already soaked and dyed wool with it. What is the law? Is the dye a separate thing on the wool, so the owner says 'Give me my dyes that you took'? Or is it not a separate thing, so the thief says 'I have nothing of yours'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a better case: the dye was already prepared, so the thief made no שינוי. Then it lays out the two sides of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the thief did not change the dye, שינוי does not settle the case. The question now seems to decide whether the owner can still demand his dye. If the dye is no longer a separate thing, the thief seems to owe nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed for (a different case)

keyTerms.term: יֵשׁ שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר
keyTerms.meaning: The dye's improvement counts as a real, separate thing on the wool
I have nothing at all of yours

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where he stole dyes already soaked, and dyed with them.
What is the law?

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר,
phrases.english: Is the dye's improvement a separate thing on the wool,
so that he (the owner) says to him:
'Give me my dyes that you took';

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא אֵין שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי הַצֶּמֶר,
phrases.english: or perhaps the dye's improvement is not a separate thing on the wool,
so that he (the thief) says to him:
'I have nothing at all of yours'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected case from Step 6 with a new one.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A thief who stole dye that was already soaked, where the owner either demands the dye itself or the thief claims he owes nothing.

steps.title: Even if the dye is gone, the thief still owes for it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. Even if the dye is no longer a separate thing, the thief cannot say he owes nothing. The owner can say: 'Pay me for my dyes that you ruined.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Even if the dye is not a separate thing on the wool, can he really say 'I have nothing of yours'? Let the owner say: 'Give me my dyes that you ruined!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects this way of framing the question. Either way, the thief has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thief who destroys stolen property still has to pay for it. So the 'nothing of yours' side was never real, and the question as framed changes nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Can he really say? (implies he cannot)
You ruined them / caused them to be lost

phrases.english: They say:

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אֵין שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר,
phrases.english: And even if the dye's improvement is not a separate thing on the wool,
can he really say to him:
'I have nothing at all of yours'?!
Let him (the owner) say to him:
'Give me my dyes that you ruined!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: וְאִי אֵין שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר, מִי מָצֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the way Step 7 framed the question.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The framing in which the owner demands the dye and the thief claims he owes nothing.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A thief must pay for stolen property he ruined, so on either side of the question the owner gets paid.

steps.title: Flipping the question: must he pay, or say 'take them'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the question around. If the dye is not a separate thing, the thief must pay. If it is a separate thing, maybe the thief can say: 'Your dye is right here in front of you; take it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, ask it from the other side. Is the dye not a separate thing, so the thief must pay? Or is it a separate thing, so the thief can say: 'Here it is in front of you, take it'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new version of the question. Now it is the thief who might gain if the dye counts as a separate thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 7 the owner gained if the dye was a separate thing. Here the thief gains, because he could say the dye still exists and hand it back as it is. If the dye is not a separate thing, it counts as lost and he must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (dropping the last idea for a new one)
To that other side (the question turned around)
Here they lie in front of you

phrases.english: Rather, ask it from that other side:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי הַצֶּמֶר,
phrases.english: Is the dye's improvement not a separate thing on the wool,
and he (the thief) must pay him;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִּלְמָא יֵשׁ שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר,
phrases.english: or perhaps the dye's improvement is a separate thing on the wool,
and he (the thief) says to him:
'Here they lie before you; take them'?
phrases.notes: The thief points to the dye soaked into the wool and says it is still there for the owner to take.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the framing rejected in Step 8 with the opposite framing.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The question is whether the thief must pay, or can tell the owner to take the dye out of the wool himself.

steps.title: You cannot get dye back out of wool
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects this framing too. How could the owner take the dye back? With soap? Soap washes the dye out, but it does not give the dye back to the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Take them'?! With what would he take them, with soap? Soap does remove the dye, but it does not give it back!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the second framing as well. The dye cannot actually be taken back, so the thief cannot say 'take them.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Returning stolen property means the owner really gets his item back. Washing dye out of wool just destroys it. So even if the dye counts as a separate thing, 'take them' is not a real way to return it, and the thief must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Returning the stolen item to its owner

steps.whatToRemember: Both framings of the dye question fail. Whether or not dye counts as a separate thing on the wool, the thief ends up paying for it.

phrases.english: 'Take them'?!
With what would he take them, with soap?
phrases.notes: Some versions have the round-bracket word; the square-bracket words are the corrected wording. Both mean 'take.'

phrases.english: Soap does remove it,
but it does not return it!
phrases.notes: Washing the dye out destroys it. The owner does not get his dye back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'take them' side proposed in Step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The thief's claim that he can return the dye as it sits in the wool.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The dye cannot be pulled out of the wool and handed back. Washing it out destroys it, so this is not a real return.

steps.title: New case: the thief stole both the wool and the dyes from one owner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the question is about a thief who stole wool and dye from the same person, dyed the wool, and now returns the dyed wool. Is he returning the dyes too, or only the wool?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, here is the case: someone stole wool and dyes from one person and dyed that wool with those dyes. Now he is giving back the wool. Does the dye count as still there on the wool, so he is returning both dyes and wool? Or does the dye not count, so he is returning only the wool and not the dyes?
steps.whatsHappening: After the earlier cases were pushed away, the גמרא offers a new case where the question about dye on wool would matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the wool and the dye belong to the same owner, and the thief gives back the dyed wool. If the dye's color counts as real (יש שבח), the owner got his dye back inside the wool. If it doesn't count (אין שבח), the thief still owes for the dye.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to set up a new case)
Or perhaps (brings in the second side of a question)

phrases.english: Rather, with what are we dealing here?
For example, where he stole wool and dyes belonging to one person,
and he dyed that wool with those dyes,
and he is returning the wool to him.

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי הַצֶּמֶר,
phrases.english: Is the improvement from the dyes on the wool something real,
so that he is returning to him both the dyes and the wool;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא אֵין שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר,
phrases.english: or perhaps the improvement from the dyes on the wool is not something real,
so he is returning the wool to him,
but he is not returning the dyes to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the soap answer in step 10 knocked out the earlier framing, the גמרא offers a new case for the question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether dye absorbed into wool counts as returned when the thief returns the dyed wool.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The question applies to a thief who stole both wool and dye from one person and returns the dyed wool.

steps.title: But the thief made the wool worth more
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: there is no real question here, because dyed wool is worth more. The owner gets the dye's value back through the higher price of the wool.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: You can settle this simply. The thief raised the value of the wool for the owner, so the owner is paid back in the price.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new case. It says the owner already gets the dye's value back, because the dyed wool he receives is worth more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the dye does not count as a real thing, the owner loses nothing. The wool's higher price covers what the dye was worth, so the question seems to make no practical difference.

phrases.english: They say:
Derive it from the fact that he raised the value
for him in price!
phrases.notes: Dyed wool sells for more than plain wool, so the owner gets paid back that way.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: תִּיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דְּאִיַּיקַּר לֵיהּ נִיהֲלֵיהּ בִּדְמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case suggested in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The practical importance of the case in step 11.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The wool's higher value already pays the owner back for the dye, so the question changes nothing.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case proposed in step 11 (a thief stole wool and dye from one owner and returns the dyed wool). The objection is that the question makes no practical difference there.

steps.title: It matters when dye prices fell, or when he dyed a basket
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the question still matters in two cases: when the dye's price dropped, or when the thief dyed a basket, where color adds no value.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed where the price of dye went down. Or if you want, say: it is a case where he dyed a basket with the dyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא saves the case from step 11 by giving two situations where the wool's higher value does not cover the dye.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If dye prices fell, the dye is now worth less than when it was stolen. The thief would rather say 'I returned your dye' than pay its old, higher value. If he dyed a basket, the color adds nothing, so the owner gets no value back unless the dye counts as returned.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (only) for this case
And if you want, say (a second answer)

phrases.english: No, it is needed where the dye went down in price.
And if you want, say:
For example, where he dyed a basket with them.
phrases.notes: Here קוֹפָא means a basket. Don't mix it up with the monkey (קוֹף) in the next step.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to situations where the higher value does not help
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Dyeing always makes the item worth more, so the owner never loses.
steps.terutzMaskana: When dye got cheaper, or when a basket was dyed, the question has a real effect on what the thief must pay.

steps.title: רבינא: a monkey dyed one person's wool with another person's dyes
steps.stepSummary: רבינא offers a different case. No thief is involved: a monkey dyed one person's wool with someone else's dyes. Can the dye owner say 'Give me my dyes'?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Here is the case. The wool belongs to one person and the dyes belong to another. A monkey came and dyed that wool with those dyes. If the dye counts as real, the dye owner can say: 'Give me my dyes, which are with you.' If it does not count, the wool owner can say: 'I have nothing of yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives a completely different case where the question about dye on wool matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because a monkey did it, no one is guilty of stealing, and the wool owner did nothing wrong. So the dye owner can only get something back if his dye still counts as existing on the wool.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
With what are we dealing here?
For example, where the wool belonged to one person and the dyes belonged to another,
and a monkey came and dyed
that wool with those dyes.

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר,
phrases.english: Is the improvement from the dyes on the wool something real,

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַב לִי סַמָּנַאי דְּגַבָּךְ נִינְהוּ;
phrases.english: so that he can say to him: Give me my dyes, which are with you;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא אֵין שֶׁבַח סַמָּנִין עַל גַּבֵּי צֶמֶר,
phrases.english: or perhaps the improvement from the dyes on the wool is not something real,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֵית לָךָ גַּבַּאי כְּלוּם?
phrases.english: and he can say to him: You have nothing with me?
phrases.notes: Here the wool owner is the one talking to the dye owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different case in place of the thief cases discussed until now.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dye owner can claim his dye back from the wool owner.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The question applies when a monkey dyed one person's wool with another person's dyes.

steps.title: Proof from ערלה: color counts as something real
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה: a garment dyed with dye from ערלה peels must be burned. This shows that the color on a garment counts as a real thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A garment that was dyed with peels of ערלה must be burned. So we see that appearance counts as something real!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question with a proof from a משנה about ערלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No one may benefit from ערלה. If the dye had vanished into the garment, there would be no reason to burn it. Since the garment must be burned, the ערלה dye must still be there as color, which shows that color is something real.

keyTerms.meaning: Fruit from a tree's first three years, which no one may benefit from

steps.whatToRemember: This proof claims that color (חזותא) counts as a real thing, which would support the side that says the dye is still there on the wool. The next step shows that רבא rejects this proof.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A garment that one dyed with peels of orlah
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in ערלה 3:1.

phrases.english: must be burned.
Apparently, appearance is something significant!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: בֶּגֶד שֶׁצְּבָעוֹ בִּקְלִיפֵּי עׇרְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question as it was set up in רבינא's case.
steps.raayaObject: That the color from dye counts as something real on the wool.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה ערלה 3:1: a garment dyed with ערלה peels must be burned.

steps.title: רבא: The Torah forbids benefit you can see
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the proof from the ערלה garment. It must be burned because the Torah forbids visible benefit, not because the dye is a real separate thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The Torah forbade benefit that can be seen with the eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on the proof from step 15. He gives a different reason why the ערלה-dyed garment must be burned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said the garment is burned because the dye is still a real 'thing' on it. רבא says the reason is different: the Torah forbids any benefit from ערלה that you can see, and colored cloth is a benefit you can see. So the ערלה case tells us nothing about whether dye counts as a real thing in the monkey case.

keyTerms.meaning: That can be seen with the eyes

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the dye is gone. He is saying the ערלה law forbids visible benefit whether or not the dye counts as a separate thing, so the proof does not work.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Benefit that is visible to the eyes
the Torah forbade

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הֲנָאָה הַנִּרְאֶה לָעֵינַיִם אָסְרָה תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 15 by giving another reason for the ערלה ruling.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the ערלה-dyed garment that dye counts as a real thing.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The burning can be explained by a special rule against visible benefit, so it does not prove the dye is a separate thing.

steps.title: A ברייתא learns that all benefit from ערלה is forbidden, including dyeing
steps.stepSummary: רבא backs up his claim with a ברייתא. The verse 'ערלים לא יאכל' adds that you may not benefit from ערלה at all, dye with it, or light a lamp with it.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: 'They shall be forbidden, it shall not be eaten.' This gives me only a ban on eating. From where do we know that one may not benefit from it, may not dye with it, and may not light a lamp with it? The verse says: 'You shall treat its fruit as forbidden... forbidden, it shall not be eaten.' This includes all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a ברייתא as his source. It shows that the Torah itself forbids dyeing with ערלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain words of the verse only forbid eating. The ברייתא reads the extra words about ערלה as adding every kind of benefit, and it names dyeing outright. So the dyed garment is forbidden by a direct verse, not because dye counts as a real thing.

keyTerms.meaning: Fruit of a tree in its first three years, which is forbidden

steps.whyThisMatters: This removes the ערלה source from the debate. The question from step 14 about the monkey and the dyes is still open.

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'Forbidden, it shall not be eaten'
I have only a ban on eating;
from where do we know one may not benefit from it,
and may not dye with it,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and may not light a lamp with it?
The verse teaches:
'You shall treat its fruit as forbidden,'
'forbidden, it shall not be eaten'
to include all of them.
phrases.notes: All three: general benefit, dyeing, and lighting a lamp.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבא's claim in step 16.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's claim that the Torah forbids visible benefit from ערלה, including dyeing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading ויקרא 19:23 as including all kinds of benefit.

steps.title: A new proof: a garment dyed with שביעית peels must be burned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries another proof. A garment dyed with peels from שביעית produce must be burned, which seems to show the dye is still a real thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A garment that was dyed with peels of שביעית produce must be burned!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a fresh proof for the question from step 14. It uses a case of שביעית instead of ערלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here no verse forbids visible benefit, so the reason seems to be that the dye is still a real piece of שביעית produce on the cloth. If that holds, color counts as a real thing, and the dye owner in the monkey case could claim his dye.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce of the seventh, Sabbatical year, which has special holiness

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A garment that one dyed with peels of seventh-year produce
must be burned!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: בֶּגֶד שֶׁצְּבָעוֹ בִּקְלִיפֵּי שְׁבִיעִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ערלה proof was rejected, the גמרא brings a different source for the same question.
steps.raayaObject: That the color on a garment counts as a real thing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A teaching that a garment dyed with שביעית peels must be burned.

steps.title: שביעית is different: it keeps its status in every form
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the שביעית proof. The verse 'תהיה' teaches that שביעית produce stays שביעית even after it changes form, so this is a special rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the verse says 'shall be.' It remains in its state.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 18 and shows why שביעית is a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'תהיה' teaches that שביעית produce keeps its holy status no matter what happens to it. So even turned into dye, the law still applies to it. This is a special rule for שביעית and does not prove that dye in general counts as a real thing.
steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs fall away. ערלה dye is forbidden because the Torah bans visible benefit, and שביעית dye because שביעית keeps its status in every form. Neither shows that color on a garment counts as a real thing.

phrases.english: It is different there,
because the verse says: 'Shall be'
it shall remain as it is.
phrases.notes: It keeps its שביעית status even after it has changed form.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the שביעית-dyed garment.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: שביעית has a special rule from the verse that it keeps its status in any form, so it cannot teach a general rule about dye.
